utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before I call for the appearances, I wish to note for the record that we are sitting today in the absence of Judge Harhoff under the provisions of Rule 15 bis. May I have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution. Does that mean we can get the documents in without any difficulty?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan, and Slobodan Zecevic appearing for Stanisic Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Igor Pantelic for Zupljanin Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. There being no preliminary matters, I'll ask the witness to return to take the stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, Mr. Djeric. I remind you that you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Djeric. We have to continue where we left off. I think that at the last session we covered at least the basic points concerning the Serbian autonomous province. However, you and I still have to establish what the constitutional basis was for its existence. You agreed that at the time you received your mandate these provinces were already in existence and operating; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So it's evident that they had a constitutional basis stemming from before the time when Republika Srpska was established; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be quite certain about that, but I know that they did exist as a constitutional category and they were regulated in a constitution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That's right. I have the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina here, and in the chapter entitled "Co-operation and association of municipalities," there is provision for a so-called city or regional association of municipalities in order to achieve certain economic and other goals. Do you know about these regional associations at the time of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Please pause before you answer. Do you remember that period?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't answer that with any precision, but I do remember there were some associations of municipalities. There were some areas covered by some chambers of commerce. So this possibility did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether you had the opportunity, as I did, when preparing for this trial, to look at the statutes of the Serb autonomous provinces which called upon this very constitutional basis for their establishment, and something struck me there in these statutes, it always says that as regards organisation and territory, they are linked to the socialist federative Republic of Yugoslavia. My question to you is the following: Could this be a result of the desire to preserve the land or fear of its loss? You spoke about this.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about the existential fear which arose when the country collapsed. As for your specific question, these constitutional facts were something I wasn't particularly interested in. I didn't deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I agree. I won't go into this any further if you haven't read the constitutions.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't actually deal with that. I didn't go into that. So when I took up my duties, these autonomous provinces already existed in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. That's sufficient. Mr. Djeric, the next area I'd like to deal with with you is the emergence of a new political organ of power or of government. It's sui generis, one of a kind organ such as had not existed before, and I'm referring to the Crisis Staffs. So you will agree with me that at the time you received your mandate the Crisis Staffs were already in existence and operating; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I don't know how far I can go with you as regards to the constitutional categories, but do you agree that these organs were envisaged in emergency situations when regular government bodies could not be constituted and could not work and that they were meant to bridge the gap that might arise in the functioning of government? Would that be a definition, in a nutshell, of the reason for their emergence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, they were established in order to carry out certain tasks when the municipal organs were unable to meet. But I'm not a lawyer. I wasn't interested in that. I was far from the party. It was the party that dealt with those things and the Ministerial Council and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, but we can't avoid this point completely, because when questioned by the Prosecutor and also in the Krajisnik case, you had to say something about those instructions and the other document withdrawing those instructions, and all of that had to do with the work of the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely how I answered the Prosecutor's question. As an elected official, I felt it my responsibility to draw the attention of those Crisis Staffs which existed, in fact -- to the fact that there were certain obligations, not just rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The purpose of my question is something you have now mentioned in the last sentence you said. You will agree with me that the Crisis Staffs began to go beyond the reasons for their existence and began to impinge on the competencies of the official state organs of government and to grab a big piece of the power which was supposed to belong to the central government authorities.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I don't know whether I need to explain this in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll go through this. I'll be putting questions to you, but you agree with me, do you not, that this would be another factor limiting the instruments of power of the central organs? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's see how far they went. So let's go through some of the decisions issued by the Crisis Staffs, and I'll put a question to you about each one.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So can the witness please be shown 1D00-0700. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I have prepared for you a binder with exhibits. If... yes. This is it. We have it in B/C/S and in English on the screen, but to spare you having to look at the monitor, I have prepared a binder for you, and the exhibits are numbered. So I'll be going through the points here by number. This is document number 1. Look at the first three items. I think they've been highlighted here. I don't know if it's the same in the English version. Here it is in B/C/S, now in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you zoom in on the first three points, and the fourth as well. It's all on the same page, so it isn't difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: As you can see, the ministry -- or, rather, the Crisis Staff is tasking the chief of the public security station with "ensuring that all decisions and conclusions of the Crisis Staff relating to the public security station be carried out within five days." And then we can see the following points. I won't read them out, but chief of the public security station is asked to explain all the decisions of the Ministry of the Interior relating to the organisation of the centre and staff appointments within the centre. And then in 3, the chief is tasked with compiling a list of assigned heads and to send it to the Crisis Staff for approval. And then in point 3, all the appointments in the public security station are considered temporary and so on. And look at four. Further tasks given to the chief of the public security station. Have you had a chance to read this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, in your government you had a Ministry of The Interior; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It had its own organisation and methods of work; is that correct? It also had its own way of appointing heads of units and so on. It had rules about this, but this, you will agree, is a direct intervention in the way of running the organ. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So the Crisis Staff is taking over powers within the hierarchy of the Ministry of Interior. Do you observe that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm sorry, but I don't think he can really answer this question either. It's a question -- anybody who can read the document can read what it says. Unless he's got inside information or knowledge of the operation of the Doboj Crisis Staff, I don't see how he can deal with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, as you say, the document speaks for itself, and I can only assume by the way that Mr. Cvijetic is proceeding that the self-evident answer that he has obtained from the witness is preliminary to something else that's relevant and admissible.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think that may be a bit optimistic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, can you please look at document number two.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for everyone in the courtroom it's 65 ter 143. Can we please zoom in on item 2, please, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, you've read item 2, and what we can see here is that the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region is setting up a police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have this document, so to say, paginated to the end until the signature? So can we look at the bottom of the page. Can we look at page 2. Yes. Thank you. And in the English version as well. Can we have page 2 in English? Ah, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, there is something that I would like to draw your attention to here. In this document and in the previous document, it doesn't say anywhere that such a decision of -- by the Crisis Staff will be conveyed to the government, to the Krajina authorities or anybody like that. Do you think that this confirms what you said earlier, that at one point you were cut off by these local regional authority that you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say several times how much the government was cut off from certain areas, the most pronounced instance of which was this one here in Doboj, the Krajina region, the Herzegovina region, and so on and so forth. Well, this is a fact, but I was not able to know about these documents. I'm seeing them for the first time. The only thing that I can be -- the only way that I can be useful here is to, let's say, express what we all knew, and that is that the governments in certain areas, these Crisis Staffs, were simply not heeding the central authorities all that much. They were themselves in power, so there was a kind of diffuse power at one point in time. I didn't know all of these particulars. All I'm saying is that there was the fact of the usurpation of power. The power was usurped, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, the reason why I'm taking you through all of these documents is among other things what you have just said. I'm also trying in these decisions to find the reasons for the adoption of that document that, like you told the Prosecutor, you signed the instructions on how the Crisis Staff can behave. So what I would like to do is show to you the range of decisions which in some way must have had to lead to that document, because their conduct needed to be regulated. So can we now look at the next document, that is document 1D00-0702. I think this is document three in your set. So we're interested in the first four paragraphs here, the numbered paragraphs. You probably had a look at this already.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for the Chamber, I just want to say we're going to cover this fast. We're for the going to stay on this for that long.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But you can see here what could be of interest later. The Crisis Staff is asking the municipality of Prijedor Public Security Station and the Prijedor Regional Command to form Intervention Squad numbering 20 men. And then in paragraphs 2 and 3 there are additional instructions issued about how that should look. And then please look at item 3 where it says: "The Municipal Crisis Staff is to give approval for the selected squad members." So a special unit is being formed, but that would be under the jurisdiction of the Crisis Staff. So it seems that as we can see at the bottom in the signature, it is not being sent to the MUP. It's not going to the government, but the whole thing remains at the local level. Do you agree with me? That is also confirms the direct interference into the process of rule by a government. I mean, it -- it just infringes on the process of work of the government. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just a second. Certainly that invites a conclusion which is for the Chamber at the end of the day. The witness shouldn't be asked that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. All right. We won't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, we will move to the next document then. We will try to find orders that deal with the financing. We're going to go in order. Can we look at 65 ter 441, please. The first two items we will shorten. We had a direct order. It's a command -- and order to commence and members of the military and regular police that, so to say, should be doing the job that they're supposed to be doing according to the law anyway? And since the law -- the Trial Chamber says that a conclusion can be drawn from this, all that remains is to be informed about this order when we come to the question and your instructions in that sense. So what we will do is move to the next exhibit, 65 ter 713. Yes. All right. Can you please look at item 2, paragraph 2. Actually, the first paragraph. Did you open the document that is five, document five in your set of documents? All right. There it is. Can you look at item 2, and you can look at the first subparagraph where it says: "Momcilo and Cedo are to settle together with Goran the matter of the public prosecutor." So the government did have a section for appointing the prosecutors, that is the Ministry of Justice?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But what we see here is that this is the interference by the Crisis Staff into the work of the Ministry of Justice pertaining to the appointment of the public prosecutor. All right, very well. I'm going to move to the next document, 65 ter 690. That is number 6 in your set of documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That last document is already an exhibit, P85.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. P85. I didn't have time to -- all right, well, we are now at 65 ter 690. Can we please open the first page. Actually, can we look at the next page. This is only the cover page of that decision. The order is inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, did you find it and the wording of the order?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's the curfew in position, a ban on movement in the Kotor Varos Municipality.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So it's a limitation or restriction of certain freedom, and the decision on that was taken by the Crisis Staff, and even when we look at the constitution and who can impose such restrictions, it's a question whether such an organ could do something like that, but it has taken it upon itself to do that. And now we're going to go through -- to the next document, that's 1D00-4513. And that is the seventh document in your set of documents. If we can look at paragraph 2 very quickly. We're not going to spend much time on this document. Item 2, have you read it? You have a direct order here for the president of the basic court and what he is to do.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So we're just going to note this as a fact, and then, finally, we're going to talk about it a little bit via your instructions. Anyway, can we look at an order, 65 ter 611. Has the order been found? Yes, I think. Let's look inside. This is just the cover page. Professor, you have it too. Can you open the next document so we can go inside into the order. I think there is the affirmation by the interpreter, and if you can skip that, that's that. Can you go inside, because we're on the cover page. Can you look at the order and see what the Crisis Staff is dealing with. "The displaced population withdrew from the Mahala, Muhici..." and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: "... is to be transferred and the military police shall provide security for the column." All right. But I think that the next document would be more important to us, so if we can just look at 65 ter 609, please. 609. Professor, that is document number 10 in your set of documents. We're interested in paragraph 1. Paragraph 1. And you can see here that the Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Sanski Most, on the basis of a proclamation by the presidents of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina Dr. Radovan Karadzic which will implement the decision on general mobilisation of forces and equipment in the republic." Have you read that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So as part of the government there is a special ministry in the government that is charged with these affairs.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So this would then infringe on the powers of a very important ministry of yours. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can we please look at 65 ter 606 now, please. Professor, that is document number 12 in your set of documents, and we're going to look at item 2. And if I can say so, here we can see the most direct interference in the affairs of the Ministry of the Internal Affairs, because the Crisis Staff is appointing and issuing a certificate or approval for Mirko Vrucinic to start work as the acting chief of the public security station. So we're going to treat this as a fact, and we're going to have the comments at the end. Mr. Djeric, the way that organs of the government and the ministries and so on were financed, how did that function at the beginning? Can you please tell us? It has nothing to do with the document. I'm just putting the question to you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the beginning, each region was financed and so on and so forth, and then there was an effort to create a single system, and this was proceeding with difficulty because the Crisis Staffs had taken over a part of those functions upon themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is precisely why I wanted to show you a document, 1D00-0769, on this particular topic. 0769. Professor, I apologise. In your binder that is document 16. We're looking at paragraph -- or item 1 in that document. That is what we are interested in. We still haven't seen it. There it is. Scroll down. Yes. It begins with the problems of financing, that paragraph. All right. Mr. Djeric, have you looked at this paragraph where it says: "The problems of financing the army and the police, it was agreed that the municipal presidents --" actually, that the financing is carried out exactly how you said in the region, that contributions were being collected. So my question on this particular topic is: This fact that the police down in the field was financed by local organs, could that fact be the reason why they directly interfered in their work, because as a rule the party that finances them perhaps feels that they have the right to set certain conditions. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just a moment. Just before -- how can he answer that question? He has no knowledge. He's been saying all throughout this that he's never seen the documents you've been showing him before. How can he possibly draw any conclusions given his state of knowledge as to whether the fact that the police were being financed by local organs means that's why they directly interfered, if indeed they directly interfered?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the point is that at sessions of the government, precisely because of this sort of behaviour by the Crisis Staffs - and I found this in the minutes - initiatives were started to abolish the Crisis Staffs. The next document I will deal with is instructions for the work of these Crisis Staffs, signed by Mr. Djeric, and we will discuss this a little bit, which attempts to introduce some order into the behaviour of the Crisis Staffs. So all these preliminary questions are leading up to the reasons for the issuing of these instructions. And who issued the instructions and why is something I want to dwell on a little bit longer with the professor. That's why I've taken the path I have leading up to these instructions for the work of the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that's fine. I mean, of course he can do that, but what he can't do is ask this witness to guess, which is what he was doing in the last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, well, then I'll ask him why these instructions were issued. Were they issued because that's how the Crisis Staffs were behaving in this way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let's deal with the instructions then. So we saw all your documents --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- and now we'll deal with your instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric -- I just have to check the number in the binder. I think it's number 17. So these are excerpts from the instructions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 97, for the Chamber. I just want to clarify two points concerning these instructions, so please bear with me for a while. 65 ter 97.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I can't but clarify this issue with you, because in my view it has remained unclarified when we link your testimony in this case with your testimony in the Krajisnik case. In that case you were shown this version of the instructions. Could we look up at the heading so we can see that it's the government that issued this. And then let's look at the last part, the last page, page 2 in both versions, Serbian and English. And the English version, too, where the signature is. You were shown this document. Evidently there is no signature and no stamp on it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, he wasn't shown this one. He was shown one of the other ones where there is a signature and stamp. Just so that Your Honours understand, there are no less than three different versions that we've got, the unsigned untyped one, one with his signature, and then it was re-issued. I think we looked at the one with the later date. So there are two signed and sealed as it were, and one blank. By mistake when we put the 65 ter list together we picked the actual unsigned one, but the others are a part of the package.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But it's the same document with which we're dealing?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is exactly the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll come to the signed one as well. I just need time to arrive at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, could you read point 13 on page 2. "War profiteers, gangs of looters, and similar ..." When the Prosecutor showed you this document, you stated very decidedly that the government could not have issued this document for two reasons. You said, first of all, because of the date, the 26th of April, 1992. You said that the government was not complete at that time and was unable to issue such a document. Am I right in stating this?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, page number for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second page of this document where the signatures are.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, the page number where you say he said this in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Djeric, saying this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that -- well, to the best of my recollection, I'm not going into these different versions of the document and so on, but the only thing I can assert is that sometime in April, early -- but -- early in April, but I can't remember exactly when, I sent the Crisis Staffs something like this, intending to draw attention to their behaviour, to warn them that they should take care. So I'm telling you now what my intention was. My intention was, in relation to these Crisis Staffs, the armed people, the people holding power, to let them know that they shouldn't behave in any way they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you say --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, no, before he goes on. It's no good making assertions such as the Prosecutor showed you this document. You said the government couldn't have issued it." I found the page number which I was asking you to give me, Mr. Cvijetic. Page 72, it's the unpaginated -- fully paginated one. "I showed him the document and he said I think it was standard practice to send them out. "Did you personally draft these instructions?" "No. Someone from the Ministry of Defence." He never at any time asserted he didn't send these -- this document out.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, as I have a sound recording of the testimony from the Krajisnik case.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did you say that this point 13 is not in your style of writing, "War profiteers, gangs of looters," and so on?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this might be contentious, but the intention was what I said, and I can confirm this. We wanted to address the Crisis Staffs concerning all these issues and let them know that they couldn't command, that they couldn't appoint officers and so on and so forth. That was what it was like at that time, because they became arrogant. They didn't trust the officers there. They wanted to replace them and so on. So that's what the idea was, the intention. As for all these different versions of documents, I can't confirm that. I can only tell you what the purpose of these documents was, but to which of these is the actual document, the real one, I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'm not trying to confuse you with these documents. Let me tell you this: I'm just trying to check the authenticity of the documents. After that I want to comment on their contents. Let me jog your memory and ask you the following: Did you say that you remember drawing up a document like this together with president Karadzic and sending it out into the field?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, correct, a document which was -- if there is a document which was signed by the president on one side and myself on the other that might be the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown document 65 ter 2341. 2341, 65 ter. Could we scroll down to where the signatures are, please. On the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, this is number 17 in your binder. So just turn the page. Yes. So we have here both the stamp and the signature, and you've said that this might be your signature when asked by the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is it the same as the previous document as regards to the content? Please read the two documents and compare them, and tell us if the content is the same or not. One of them is in slightly larger letters.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they seem to be the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that they're identical?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they appear to be identical, yes. I can't now take the time to compare every word, but they seem to be identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. What I'm interested in now, Professor, is the following: When we read the content of this excerpt from the instructions, my impression is that the author evidently had the intention of regulating and disciplining the behaviour of the Crisis Staffs. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is the entire purpose, to somehow let the Crisis Staffs know that they couldn't behave irresponsibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, to put it briefly. However, the next document, 65 ter 105 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have it on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's 18 in your binder, Professor. Only four days later -- have you found the document? This is a letter withdrawing these instructions. How would you explain the fact that the instructions were withdrawn after four days?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not clear to me. I answered the question by the Prosecutor here. This was not my practice to withdraw an instruction that was sent out, especially not in such a brief period of time. I simply don't understand this. It's not clear to me. I can't remember. This was towards the end of April. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had already been established then. The Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina issued its decision on the withdrawal of the army, but I simply don't know. As I said, this was not my usual way of working. It wasn't my practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as these documents all hang together and the professor here is their author, I tender them into evidence. First is 65 ter 97. The second is 65 -- well, 65 ter 97, that's the first excerpt I showed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Are there any of these which are not already exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I -- which documents? Are you just trying to tender the ones, the excerpt ones? No, Your Honours, what's happened is -- I don't think anybody is tendering exhibits at the moment because you haven't admitted any of ours until you've heard cross-examination. It's all sitting in this wonderful amorphous way somewhere above this court. So I'm not trying to -- I don't know how this is going to work now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just give me a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay, okay, okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I assist though? 97 was exhibited. It's actually P70. It must have come in some other way. And the other document that Mr. Cvijetic has referred to may be part of the package that went in with the 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, and the registry agrees with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So that's where we are with that. Marked for identification --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- and we'll see where we go with the facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do we have the 65 ter number of that second document?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, it was a hundred --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's 105, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 105, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, the 65 ter package did go in as an exhibit. 65 ter. 92 ter. Is that right? Exactly, so that is already an exhibit and part of the transcript, and the other one went in --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yeah, 105's on the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have noted that the 65 ter 97, that it's now P70. Is that correct? And the next document is the signed version of the same excerpt, 65 ter 2341, and I haven't noted that it's been -- that it's been tendered into evidence as a Prosecution exhibit. Has it been admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. But the point is nobody, as I understand it, is getting anything admitted with this witness until everything has been dealt with. Otherwise, it doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P2341 was admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: With another witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, as part of the package.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the third one is the 65 ter document 105.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is one --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, you have thus no explanation why within four days you would withdraw such an instruction. So let us try maybe to solve the mystery.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness 65 ter 145, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, that is number 19 in your binder. I'm sorry for not letting you know that in time, but we'll take it slowly. As you can see, this is a decision by the Presidency on the formation of War Presidencies in municipalities in times of the immediate threat of war or time of war. You know about that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't remember that, because this was done by Karadzic. I mean, this is his segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Can you please look at item 2. Perhaps you will refresh your memory, where it says that: "The War Presidency shall consist of a representative of the republic and, generally, a commissioner --" Did anybody ask you about any of these matters in the previous case?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency as the coordinating body did this, and it constantly did have representatives from the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we now please look at Article 5. And in the B/C/S, Professor, you've already found this. Article 5. It's on the left side of the page. That's right. Article 5. I thing you've found it. I think in the English also we need to see Article 5. In paragraph 2 it says -- have you found it? "The day the War Presidencies are established, the Crisis Staffs shall cease to operate in municipalities across the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Professor, I'm going to come out with a thesis and let us see if you agree with that. Were the Crisis Staffs at all under the jurisdiction of the government or anyone?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staffs have nothing to do with the government. They were formed by the party and then they continued to work on their tasks. These representatives also, they were not an organ of the government in any shape or form.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. My next question, that instruction of yours, then, can it be considered as, let's say, an attempt by you or the government to regulate an area that had escaped control and that it turned out that it was actually not part of your duties and that you had to give that to the Presidency, so you didn't pursue that to the end? This is my assumption.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. This is all under the jurisdiction of the services in the government. This is a kind of legal affairs subject matter. So it regulates the subject matter the way it regulates the subject matter, and then the government issues instructions in a certain way, and then they can be placed in a different context. I told you, and this is what I remember, that I sent simply to the Crisis Staffs, and I think that even Karadzic signed that, so this was very early in April -- early in April, because it -- the times were like that, you know. It was simply that there was a major diffusion of power. The situation was very raw and so on and so forth. So much of the subject matter was unregulated. So everything is possible. And in the context of what you answered, I am saying that the practice, unless there was force majeure or this legal aspect of it, it wasn't the practice to recall anything. This wasn't done.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you are allowing for this possibility?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am allowing for the possibility that a Presidency, because that was authorised for these matters, that things proceeded in this particular way and then that that reflected in turn on the things that happened. I allow that as a possibility. I allow that possibility, but I really couldn't swear an oath here and say, yes, I definitely remember this or that. I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, I did state that as a possibility.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but for reasons of force majeure perhaps, yes, it's possible that this was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to confirm this possibility with you in a different way, not only through this document by the Presidency but also differently. You will agree that in themselves the Crisis Staffs could not fit into the system of authority at the top of which was the government under any of the organs that you were at the head of?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And I see in the second reason that you withdrew that instruction and allowed the Presidency to deal with that. Is that assumption of mine correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what can happen is that the government was formed and that the ministries were doing their job, and then this dealing with the Crisis Staff was left to the Presidency, and it was maintaining contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When you mention this word "to deal with them," do you have the information how long the Crisis Staffs functioned in certain areas of Republika Srpska? Do you have information about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from what I can remember at this point that there were plenty of differences. It varied from staff to staff and from SAO to SAO areas. The regions in the east accepted the government fairly quickly, and so on and so forth. There were some problems with Herzegovina, but the most resilient was the Krajina Autonomous Region, and their work. They managed to persevere all the way until the autumn, and they were the most persisted in that. Even I myself asked myself several times who did this suit? I mean, it must have suited somebody for the situation to be maintained in that way. They persevered until the autumn and were quite strong. And since this was the largest region, territorially and by population, perhaps it comprises some 70 to 80 per cent of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they simply believed there that the Crisis Staffs and that region considered itself enough unto itself and it behaved the way it behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Mr. Djeric, did you have information that some Crisis Staffs had called themselves War Staffs and even the presidents called themselves the commanders of the staffs? Just please wait for this to be entered into the transcript. All right. You can go ahead now. Did you have that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember at this point in time what they called themselves, but they did have the power. They did declare themselves this president or that president, war president, commanders, and that they were carrying out command duties and deciding on personnel policies and some cadre matters. Well, yes, we knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So then we can conclude that Crisis Staffs, after the Serbian autonomous regions or parallel with them, were the second most important factor that limited or restricted the instruments of central authority in the form of the government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the form of the government and all the other organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, all right, but we primarily are thinking of the government. I think that we have dealt sufficiently with the Crisis Staffs.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know if it's time for a break. I'm preparing to move to a different topic, so perhaps this would be a good moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]. You have another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I would like to now move to, and let me say move closer to the Ministry of Internal Affairs, if I can put it that way. In order for the ministries in the government to have some sort of indication of what they were supposed to do, what they were supposed to be dealing with, and what was under their jurisdiction, it was important to have not only the laws but also some government guidelines so that they would be issued with some direction and instruction for 1992. Do you recall a document called "The Operative Programme of Measures to Prevent the Disruption of Social Flows in the -- in Wartime Conditions"? This is the title of the document. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at document 20 in your set of documents then. And that is 1D00-0552. Mr. Djeric --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: -- on first on the first page, and the Chamber can see it as well, this is a document -- actually, this is a cover letter accompanied -- accompanying that programme so that the ministry could state its remarks or comments on that document. Can you recall that document perhaps?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible, because certain documents are being referred to here that should be adopted, certain legal gaps need to be bridged. More or less it's all in the spirit of the work of the government before the conflict broke out. The actual title, "Operational Programme of Measures to Prevent the Disruption of Social Flows in the Condition of," you know, so on and so forth. "Disruption of Social Interactions in Times of War." That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Can we now please enter this document if the interpretation is finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And can we look at the B/C/S page, Professor, 2, page 2. Now, I must parallelly open that document. That is document number 20. This is page number 4 in the English version, item 4. It's a very important document, so we will not go fast. And we have the English version -- great, you've found it. And the B/C/S version you've also found. I'm going to give you some time to read the document. So one of the tasks was to adopt a law on state administration, and you can see the text where it says that the question of responsibility would need to be focused on, all of your organs, ministries, were actually administration organs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And the regulations on the matters of -- regulations applied to them that regulated the work of the administration organs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at item 8 now, please, in the BH version. It's on page 2 and -- 3. It's on page 3. And then in the English version it's on page 5. Page 5 in the English, paragraph 8. Can we scroll up, please. And then it goes on to the next page, so then we will have to ... In English it is on two pages, and the title is "Development of Wartime Organisation and Specification of Jobs." And then we can move to the next page in the English version to see what this is about. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, did you read item a little bit? So this is an instruction to all the ministries and the republican organs to draft their own wartime organisation and job specification, which implies a transition to wartime operations, implying that the minimum number of employees would need to be established and so on. So my question is: Professor, what regulations are the source for this particular instruction?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember. I don't remember even -- I think that simply there was a problem constantly in the government, a kind of discrepancy between the normative basis and the situation in the field. Thus we simply had peacetime laws and regulations, and on the other hand, we had a fierce conflict which was obvious. So what this boiled down to was -- well, Sarajevo, Mr. Izetbegovic. Mr. Izetbegovic declared a state of war, whereas in the republic of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina there was no state of war, and the whole basis of the regulations was peacetime regulations. So -- I mean, you can say that we were thinking of appointing a Presidency that was in his domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said to be -- to provide this for the -- to the president.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government could not declare a state of war. From time to time there were meetings where such an issue was discussed. It was tabled, and it was brought to the attention of the political leadership, but it was resolutely against declaring a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, I'm going to be specific. This obligation not only of the government organs but all the state organs stemmed from the law All Peoples Defence, which provided for the adoption of these regulations, the so-called wartime plans, job specifications, and so on. Am I right in that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's something else. This is in the event of war the ministry had the duty, the Ministry For Defence, to provide these documents and so on and so forth. And to move or transfer the entire economic system to a wartime economic system.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the duty of all of those wartime subjects to have wartime plans.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is something else again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The question is specific, Professor. Did all the organs have to have these specific plans?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. This was their duty under the constitution. In the event of war, they had the wartime --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Plans.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- plans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, it's that time now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We're now dealing with the same document. I just need the sixth page in the B/C/S version, and in the English version it's page 18. Point 18. Page 6 in B/C/S, point 18. Yes, that's it. And in the English version, on page 10, point 18. That's it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, have you found it? Page 6.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Point 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. In this operative programme, there is a certain task for the Ministry of the Interior which is to issue regulations on the internal organisation of the ministries in wartime conditions. Is that right? And here it says what such a document should contain; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So we will just take note of the fact that this is an obligation undertaken, and we'll comment on it later on. You will agree that this obligation follows from the same regulations we've already referred to. Is that right? Could we now move on to page 7 in B/C/S. That's point 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 11 in English. The next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And here we see a brief order intended for the Ministry of the Interior on excluding from traffic all motor vehicles without proper documentation. And when we come to this, we will refer to this obligation of the ministry. Let's just see what was the ministry's task. Let's move to page 8 in B/C/S and page 12 in the English version. And we'll dwell on this a while. Professor, you're on page 8, are you not? On the left-hand side. Yes, that is where it begins.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In English we're on page 12 and page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, we have a complex task here, an order to both the Ministry of the interior and the Ministry of Justice and also the Ministry of Defence. So I would like to focus now on items 2 and 3. In item 2 it says that in co-operation with the judicial state organs, the military judicial organs and the organs of the ministry police, activities should be stepped up on discovering and bringing in perpetrators of misdemeanors and crimes, especially with a view to suppressing thefts, war profiteering, and other criminal actions. So this is a common task for all. And then we have item 3, which is perhaps even more interesting here. "Within the scope of their activities, the ministry and its services should establish organised access to work on gathering and processing data and documentary evidence, materials on genocide and war crimes against the civilian population." So I'll dwell on this a while longer. I will try to remind you of your testimony on Friday. You said that at the government you discussed the issue of war crimes and genocide and that you did not discuss only crimes against Serbs. You did not discuss these things collectively. It doesn't say which population. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said, and I can confirm it again. There was discussion of this at the government, and orders were issued to the appropriate ministries more than once, especially the Ministry of the Interior and the Ministry of Justice, that they should take measures and prosecute all those who violated the law and international laws and regulations, humanity, and so on. That's certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a second.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is stressed in this document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me just highlight "Documentary Materials on Crimes That Have Been Perpetrated." So there is a duty to keep records of these crimes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, now that we're dealing with this, let me ask you this: Can you recall who gave the initiative that work should be done on collecting this documentary material?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall specifically, but I know that these conclusions were reached at the government session and that the government then tasks the ministries with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll come back to this. And in this context I'd like to move on to item 27. Professor, that's on page 9 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Point 27 in English, it's on page 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That's point 27. I think we've found it. Professor, as you've seen, a state commission is to be appointed to establish crimes and genocide against the civilian population and victims of war, and this is a task given to the Ministry of Justice; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We have to bring this into the context of the previous conclusion by the government, and you will agree that there is no selective approach here either.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Crimes are universal, and a state commission was to be appointed to deal with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I hope that this has jogged your memory a little bit. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after all these years it's good to have your memory jogged.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you about something else that has to do with this operative programme so you can be sure what we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have document 65 ter 929.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This -- these should be minutes of the 41st session of the government, and then we'll look at the agenda, and after that point 1. The agenda is on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in English I think it can only be on page 1 or 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Point 1. Professor, you have to look at the screen. You don't have this in your binder. At the government session of the 29th of July, 1992, this proposal of the operative plan or programme, as we've called it, was on the agenda. You can see that, can't you? And if you look further, after discussion of the agenda on pages 2 and 3, and mostly on page 4 - I don't know if you can follow - there is a small discussion in which suggestions are made. So let's go one page forward. The B/C/S version, page 4. No? Yes. Here we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's just find the right place in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And it says here: "The following observations and comments were made on the proposed text." I think we're on the right page. Excellent. And here, Professor, we can see that members of the government are making their suggestions and their comments on this proposed text. And as you can see here, it was concluded that possible suggestions should wait until the final text so that the instructions can be further elaborated. Can you see that? You have a passage here. I'll read it out. It says: "The government has again pointed out the need to establish co-operation between the departments and ministries in the process of preparation and proposals of the appropriate regulations." So we won't deal with this session anymore, but we'll conclude that the government monitored the implementation of this programme at its sessions. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Amongst other things, one of the orders by the MUP was, as we saw, to work on the uncovering of crimes and the legal processing of perpetrators and so on and so forth. I particularly emphasise organised crime, looting, robbery, and so on. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. This was quite prominent for the reason that the crime which was rampant was undermining the authority, the government, especially if ministers or parts of the state administration were actually taking part in such activities. That is why we were paying particular attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In light of that, I'm going to dwell now on some tasks that were part of the job of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at document 1D00-0496, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, that is document 21. The government, or you as the prime minister, signed the order that was sent to Cedomir Kljajic at the Ministry of the Interior, and he was to have submitted a report on the security of people and property in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina, and then you referred to an incident with the passenger cars -- or actually, TAS vehicles, and you had some part in that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember. I can see that the document was signed by Deputy Prime Minister Trbojevic on my behalf. But I do remember the problem, I do. The government had charged the authorised ministry to draft a report in this case about this, but generally the practice was for the ministry to be charged with providing information on the security of persons and property, and you can see that we were particularly focusing on the task products. Madam Prosecutor asked me a few days ago, and she placed things in a certain context, and I can say that we did everything, we did everything to keep the factory working, because it was important for us for the TAS car factory in Sarajevo to keep working, because it happened to be a source of industrial production pride in Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina, and other than that, we wanted to maintain production and the production of cars for fiscal reasons, because how can the government work if companies don't pay regular tax? And I made a considerable effort, and all the company representatives know that. They know that. I mean, their reports need to be looked at, who did how much and what efforts were invested to protect the factory. And in any case, at least to try to compensate for a part of the damages that were inflicted. I can -- I mean, I can speak much more about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm going to deal with that through specific questions, but for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, I would like to explain. The abbreviation is Tvornica Automobila Sarajevo. Sarajevo car factory, TAS. So we're going to use the abbreviation.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a Volkswagon car manufacturing plant.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And Golf passenger cars were assembled in that plant, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The task issued by the government --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at document 65 ter 1398.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's report by inspectors of the Romanija-Birac CSB centres, whose assignment it was to go and investigate what was happening in that factory. On page 1 I'm going to draw your attention to paragraph 2, where it says -- here we are on the first page now. That: "On the same day when we arrived, a meeting was organised by the Vogosca leadership, representatives of the military authorities, and the judiciary, by the prison authorities, and it was also attended by chiefs of the public security stations and the commands." And then a couple of sentences later on the same page it is noted that the criminal investigation service -- there was no service in the Vogosca station, and particularly of concern was the occurrence of theft of cars from the compound of the TAS factory. Then the inspectors note that there is a suspicion about the legality of the transactions that had to do with the removal of the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at page 2 in the Serbian version. It's also on page 2 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, this is the paragraph in the middle, and it begins on the date -- with the date, on the 6th of July. Let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're still not on the document in the English version. Oh, we are on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: There is an interesting remark here, Professor, by the inspectors. They say that representatives of the basic court from Sarajevo came to Vogosca. The prosecutor, the public prosecutor, representatives of the Ministry of Justice both from Sarajevo, with whom it was previously agreed that they would come and stay for some time in order to carry out work from their jurisdiction. And so if you can now pay attention to the following assertion: The representatives left the following day in three new passenger vehicles, Golf model ones, saying on that occasion that they had completed their task. Evidently the inspectors had a much more difficult task than it would seem at first glance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the of the report, the last five lines before the signature. We can already see it in English. If we can just scroll down in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, you're at the end of the document; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We can see something quite interesting here, and it says: "In addition, the meeting expressed an opinion that the staffing policies of the Vogosca SJB can be conducted only by the SJB chief and his workers collective, and no one from the MUP or the municipality could appoint people to this service. "In addition, it was said at the meeting that we were now persona non grata, and there was no need for us to be there. We should have come earlier and so on." In your opinion does this seem to you to be the remnant of the local influence on the police stations due to which the Ministry of Internal Affairs evidently has problems to discipline the station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Here you have the most telling examples of how this persisted relatively. Here we are in July --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, apparently Ms. Korner has given up on objecting to this line of questioning, but how does it assist -- how does this assist the Chamber whose responsibility it is at the end of the day to make decisions? How does specifically in this case this witness's opinion on a document that he had nothing to do with at all, apparently of a site visit to this car factory that he wasn't even a part -- where is this taking us?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this report and all the subsequent ones on the factory were drafted pursuant to orders and assignments issued by the government and the prime minister to the MUP to investigate an affair. So the whole matter is being presented through this witness. This is what I'm trying to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, I will -- I will repeat my objection again. The question that he was asked on this was: "In your opinion, does this seem to be the remnant of the local influence on the police stations due to which the Ministry of Internal Affairs evidently has problems to discipline the station?" This witness does not know from Adam what this is a remnant of. He got the report, that's it, if he got the report at all. So he cannot deal with that, and his answer is absolutely worthless, Mr. Cvijetic, because it's no more than a guess than anybody else in this court can do. And I hope that's clear, and I'm going to -- I stopped repeating the objection because it wasn't getting anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The witness confirmed that this was a remnant of such occurrences and that he knows that there were such local influences on the local stations. But, Your Honours, here I will agree. I'm not going to ask the witness to provide comments of this kind, but I am going to go through the reports until we get to the final outcome of the investigation, because that was an assignment issued by the Ministry of the Internal Affairs and which -- to the MUP and which it carried out, and it is said in the operational programme that they should deal with organised crime, and then there is a specific order here to resolve a particular affair that has to do with that kind of activity, and I would like to throw some light on that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The witness should be asked: "Did you see this whole series of reports at the time or subsequently?" If the answer is no, then he can't do anything else but comment on contents in the same way as anybody who reads them can. So that is the first question that has to be asked before this tedious procedure can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course I will [microphone not activated] any decision, any of your rulings, but Mr. Djeric did not recognise even his own presence in some meetings that were shown to him at the Presidency, but he did comment on the content of the meeting and the minutes or the agenda, actually, the agenda. Very well. I'm going to wait for your decision before I continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Cvijetic, please continue if only because the -- we are likely to reach the end of this exercise more quickly without having to give rulings on each of these objections, verbalised or not, which your line of questions invite.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm going to skip a few documents. I'm going to just show 65 ter 305 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Since we're talking -- we see here that the 47th session of the government is being referred to, held on the 20th of August, 1992, where the prevention of crimes was discussed. The minister of the interior on the occasion of that meeting -- this is document 25 in your -- in your set of documents. Document 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a mistake in the transcript. It should be 65 ter 306, document 306.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a misunderstanding. I did say 65 ter 306, but it came out differently in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, as a result of the discussion at the government session, the minister became involved and established the deadline by which this affair had to be investigated. Do you remember the session at which this was discussed?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but as to details --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The minister refers to the task he received at the government session.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And he establishes a deadline by which the investigation should be completed. My question is the following: Do you know what was ultimately discovered? What happened concerning these vehicles? Do you remember how the affair ended?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the details, but the whole problem was to find out what had happened with these vehicles. They seemed to have sprouted wings and flown here and there. Who took possession of these vehicles? Who played a role in all this? Because we knew at the time that the commercial enterprises which had paid for the vehicles were looking for ways to retrieve these vehicles, not to mention all the vultures from the region which had gathered around that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the last document which might throw some light on what we're talking about. It's 65 ter 1350. Professor, it's under the same number, the last document. Did you have occasion to see this letter of the republican commissioner, Nikola Poplasen?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Addressed to the War Presidency of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not, but I can explain how this came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I complained to the political top saying that things could not be done in this way and that they should intervene, and then the commissioner went there, too, and I suppose that's how this letter came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And we can see from the letter that the sale was being done in order to obtain means for Vogosca; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Either for hard currency or goods we're interested in, and the ministry of the economy should be tasked with this, with the tasks and Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So while the ministry was carrying out the investigation, on the 24th of June these vehicles were sent with this purpose.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't say with what purpose, because it follows from this letter that that was the intention, that some of the vehicles went for other purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But this last document does contribute to clarifying the affair, does it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were cars found in storage, and everybody tried to profit by this, and the local officials in Vogosca, as you can see, ensured the command of the army in this way. I'm now speaking based on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But the truth came to light owing to the investigation carried out by the ministry; is that correct? All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a letter from the commissioner, Commissioner Poplasen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the line of the Presidency now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: From the document issued by the government, there was another obligation following from that for the ministry to inform the government on the security situation, the security of people and property, and the general security situation in the republic. Do you remember that this was in the document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have document 65 ter 176, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: In your case it's document 26.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Document 26, information on certain aspects. Well, just please wait a minute until we find this on the screen. So the Ministry of the Interior, and in the heading we see that it is delivering to the president of the government and the president of the Presidency, information on certain aspects of work carried out up to that point and tasks ahead. Have you looked at the document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll -- I'll give you time to look through it. As it's addressed to you directly, please look right through it. It might jog your memory. We'll go through some passages. I'll be putting questions.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember this particular document, but I do know that these orders and these tasks were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And this would be a response to some of those orders. We'll dwell on a few examples.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This mentions information, some aspects of the work done to date and tasks ahead, and we asked information on the security of property and of persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you agree that we look inside the document to see whether it contains a response to your question? We can open the first page. The page right after the title page. Yes. It's already open both in the English and the Serbian versions. So I'll ask you, first of all, Mr. Djeric, do you know about this meeting in Belgrade where the minister gathered all the chiefs of the security services together for the first time? You spoke of the problems people had in travelling, and there was a meeting of the collegium of the police in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there certainly were problems in travelling, getting from one place to another. And as for this meeting, I don't really see why it should have been held in Belgrade. Why did it have to be in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, the policeman explained why. It was a central point where everybody was able to travel at that point. But let's look at --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it shouldn't have been done that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. On the first page the minister is providing information, saying that a good part of the police force, and he says the same on the next page, has been mobilised and used for military purposes. You can see that on pages 2 and 3 as well. And that this is hindering the completion of the basic tasks of the police. Were you aware of the use of the police force for wartime purposes, and did this really happen?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the police were used for war purposes. This is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Who was in charge of that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
