utterances.text: The president, the army, and so on. The police could be resubordinated to the army and the vertical chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's it. Let's now move to page 3 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't agree that the mobilisation component could make it impossible for the remainder of the ministry to do their job.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. Let's take it step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version we're on page 3, and we're also on page 3 in the Serbian version. So in the B/C/S version it's the fourth paragraph, and in the English version it's also the fourth paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Attention is drawn to the fact here that neither the military nor the civilian judiciary is functioning, that Judges have not been elected, that several thousand court cases remain unresolved in the Bosnian Krajina, that there are no Judges to deal with criminal cases, that they're intimidated, that they are being threatened and so on, that hardened criminals are being released from gaol, and all this is affecting the establishment of the rule of law and the work of the ministry. So this topic has been broached in this report. Do you know about these problems in the functioning of the judiciary organs, especially the military ones, and did you discuss this at the government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were problems in the beginning initially, and then in June, I think, a decision was reached to establish military courts, a military prosecutor's office, the military judiciary organs. Yes, that is true, and in this passage it talks about the problems I had as the president of the government. You see, there were problems in the judiciary. These two ministries were always being highlighted as the key ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Now that you've mentioned the military judiciary organs, are you aware that in the division of competencies war crimes fell under the jurisdiction of the military courts and were tried there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak about these competencies here, but what I do know is that all these problems concerning the judiciary were under the care of Mr. Trbojevic. He was in charge of dealing with all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to page 4 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And we're on page 3 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Let me just see. In the Serbian version it's paragraph 2 on page 4. Let's just wait until we find the English version. And on page 3 it's the fifth paragraph in the English version. Page 3, paragraph 5. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Four, paragraph 2. Please read it. "It was pointed out that the priority for both the national service and the crime investigation service, that's the MUP is to detect war crimes, provide documentation and file criminal reports, documents also provided for war crimes committed by Serbs."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already mentioned that. No distinction was drawn. All crimes had to be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: When you say that the government asked for this to be done, it also refers to the organ tasked with this area. If you agree, let's look at page 6.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. If this is an opportunity for me to speak about this, I'll speak about it now. The government kept asking for this to be done, but this was kept back at the level of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We'll deal with that in due course. Page 6, Professor, of the Serbian version, the second paragraph. And page 4 in the English version, paragraph 5. Here you have a statement saying that the Ministry of the Interior is a professional police with no influence from politics, individuals and groups, and so on. And then reference is made to a decision of the Presidency of the Srpska Republika saying that no party activities should be carried out in the police. It seems that the government at one of its sessions issued the conclusion that in wartime conditions, and when there is an imminent threat of war, all political activity should be stopped. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that the government issued this conclusion and insisted with the political leadership that this should be strictly respected, because there would have been huge problems if political parties had continued being active in these institutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It says that: "Our work is professional work within the scope of the work of the Ministry of the Interior on establishing the rule of law," and so on. So attention is drawn to professionalism in the work of the organs of the Ministry of the Interior, and this had the support of the government. Is that right? You're not listening to me, Professor. So there is government support.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already answered that. The government supported that long before. That was the context in which they were operating.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We are now on page 7 of the Serbian version, paragraph 1. And we are on page 4 of the English version, the last paragraph. So in accordance to the operations plan of the government, we have anti-crime combat here as one of the primary goals. Is that correct, Professor? Regardless of the perpetrators. Are you on the correct page? Page 7, paragraph 4, I think. So the variant of this position you can also find on page 8 of the Serbian version. And now we're going to see where that is in the English version. In the English version this is page 5, the last paragraph, the paragraph but last. Have you found that there? It's the last paragraph on page 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the English we have it, and we should be on the eighth page in the Serbian version, last paragraph. Scroll up. Scroll up. Thank you. Yes, the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, you can see the tasks which should constantly be insisted upon include prevention and detection of crimes and their perpetrators with emphasis on the most serious crimes regardless of the perpetrators." It seems to me that - how can I put it -- it fits in with the policies of the government that we talked about.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did talk about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And there is a separate conclusion on page 9 by the ministry. It's page 9, one paragraph but last.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in the English version this is on page 6, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And this is what we talked about, the prevention and documenting of war crimes. This is paragraph 3 on this page. So documenting of war crimes, and in the professional sense what is stated here is how it will be documented and who is going to participate in that. So pursuant to what was said in the operative programme, the ministry had already specified the practical measures to implement that in this conclusion, Professor.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is material that only expresses wishes and intentions, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Can you now look at page 11, please, paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that we are on page 6 of the English version, the last sentence down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Professor, the ministry here has touched upon financial -- financing matters, and I think we have now come to the question that we have touched upon before with the Ministry of the Internal Affairs where it says that it has to be financed exclusively from the budget of Republika Srpska and so on and so forth. You talked a little bit about that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And the reasons for that. I'm only asking you about that, not only in relation to this document, but you personally as the prime minister, the reasons why it's essential for an organ as important as this to be financed from the central budget. What are they?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, any police in the world or any MUP is financed from the budget, because it's an organ of the public administration, a part of the government of the state, and it cannot be financed on a day-to-day, case-by-case basis, you know. But this paragraph here is interesting, and the reasons for that is that the ministry, and primarily the minister, understood that the Ministry of the Internal Affairs and the police has to be financed from the budget but not in the way that he thought of previously, not by confiscating property and wherever they can get their funds on. I mean, we had a dispute about that. Simply there were certain practices that were directly favoured by the minister but which actually deviated from this manner of financing, and then he understood that he could not do it any other way than the proper way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But he understood that and then he issued the order?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did understood that, and then -- he did understand that, and that's what it says here, but the government, I remember, we did deal with that matter and there were open disputes about that where the minister was told that he could not do things in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And as you can see, this was effective, and in the material it says that he did --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Take measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: -- take measures. All right. Very well. I don't know how we are for time, but one of the tasks from the operative programme was for the ministry to adopt certain documents so that organ could be forced to adhere to regulations. So it's not enough only to have the law on the internal affairs, but it was necessary also to adopt some internal documents, and I did find somewhere that it was you who insisted that things be done to that effect, and so I would just like to list the documents that the minister managed to adopt in that period in spite of all of his commitments. So we're not going to deal with the professional part of that set of documents. I will show you just some regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at exhibit 1D50. Yes. We will not enter the document. We are just going to list to see how many of these documents the minister adopted. We're not going to look at all them. We will just see. Yes, here.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, you can see here the minister adopted, amongst other things, the instructions on the rules of behaviour and interpersonal relations of the personnel of the Ministry of the Interior. Namely, this is an instruction that the police refers to as the code of conduct of policemen. I don't know if you had any access to these normative activities of the ministry, but I am going to list for you what the minister adopted in that period, internal documents.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course I didn't have access to the internal documents of the ministry. I really --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] "I'm going to list for you the documents that are produced." Well, how is this going to take us anywhere? How can this witness comment on documents he's never seen before? And he appears to be nodding in agreement. There must be some control over where cross-examination goes, Your Honours, with the greatest of respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have any intention of dealing with the actual document and for the witness to interpret them in the professional sense, because I know he's unable to do that, but I'm letting him know that according to the operational programme of the government, the ministry was obliged to adopt these documents. The documents have been admitted as exhibits, and all I wish to do is to list to the witness how many documents the minister adopted acting pursuant to the instructions of the government. I don't wish to discuss the substance of the documents. I just wish to prove that the operative programme duties were actually fulfilled and met. This is what I want to prove, only that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is not the time to prove anything, nor does the Defence have to prove anything. The point of having a witness there is to ask the witness questions about matters on which he can comment or put to him matters which are not accepted by the Defence. We haven't even remotely begun to get near what this witness has said about Mr. Stanisic himself. Now, Your Honours, I do object to this. I don't think Mr. Cvijetic has grasped the fact that you don't just show a witness things, you ask a witness questions either to get information from him or, alternatively, to contradict what he said in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before you make the decision, can we discuss this without the presence of the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The difficulty that the Chamber's facing, Mr. Cvijetic, is what Mrs. Korner has just articulated in her -- the last part of her submission is something that we have lost count of the number of times in today's session that -- the point that we have made, and yet your persist in dealing with these documents in this manner, and I quite frankly don't know what -- what else to say. The -- as I said earlier, it seemed to me at some point that rather than trying to interrupt you that we would get through this painful exercise more quickly if you were just allowed to continue, but the Chamber is prepared to accept that you as -- to presume, I should say, that as counsel you have a point initially as to where -- even if it isn't apparent to us, but when it becomes patent that the witness is being asked -- offer comments of documents that are just being dumped in, as Mrs. Korner has, with respect, correctly said, we must draw a line some place.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If we can just have the witness go out so that we can explain what we mean. We don't want to keep the witness. We wish to discuss this a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If you think that would assist. Mr. Djeric, we are about to take a break in about five minutes, so you're excused a little ahead of that. We would -- we would resume with you in 25 minutes. So you're excused from the chamber for the time being.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cvijetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like this, Your Honours: In reference to the assertion by the witness from his previous testimony that Mr. Stanisic in some way was not under the control of the prime minister, that he was closer to the Presidency than to the government, and so on and so forth, we have started to pursue a line proving the opposite, that Mr. Stanisic was a minister in that government, that as the minister in that government all the tasks that he got from the government he regularly fulfilled, and even though -- and those who got from the president personally and from the government, and all those tasks that were given to him through the government's operational programme he fulfilled them. So I have embarked on proving those issues. So the assertion by Mr. Djeric that can be boiled down to just saying that the minister was not seen by him often, that he was often or mostly with the president, the only way to deal with that assertion is to show Mr. Djeric documents and what that minister did in these conditions, whereby we will prove that he was a member of the government indeed, and that as a minister in that government he completely fulfilled his duties in accordance with the law and his powers. We believe that this is a real way of disputing his plain statement that things were not like that. We could also say that what he's saying is not true, but this is something that you would not accept. So the only realistic way is to demonstrate through using and showing you documents that that is not correct. That is our objective.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: No. I was going to say that that is -- I understand everything that you have said. My -- what I'm having difficulty with is where the documents that you -- on which you're seeking to rely have and on the face of it no connection with the witness and when the witness indicates he knows nothing about it, never seen it before, mustn't you abandon the line on that particular document and move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, precisely this witness signed the operative plan and programme that instructed the minister to adopt all of these documents. So how can I now not use the opportunity to show him that the minister did act according to his instructions and adopted all of those documents, instructions, books of rules, remember the rules on internal operations, disciplinary regulations and so on. So the only way I can dispute his assertions is to show him documents. We don't have to deal with the substance of the documents with the witness, and this is not what I'm going to -- I'm just going to list the instructive acts and documents that the minister adopted. I'm just going to list them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, what Mr. Cvijetic is doing is giving evidence. It is not for him to list documents to a witness. Mr. Stanisic, if he decides to give evidence, or when his interview goes in, can -- will be dealing with all of this. He is the person who did, or one of the other officers. This witness cannot deal with it. All he can say to the witness is, "I suggest to you that you are wrong," or however he puts it when you say that Mr. Stanisic did not carry out the tasks. It is then for him in a proper manner not as I suggest what is now an improper manner of reading lists of documents to the witness to establish that this witness may be wrong. In fact, this witness did not say -- and this whole line of cross-examination is misconceived. He didn't say that Mr. Stanisic didn't do his job. His complaint was that Mr. Stanisic did not turn up to meetings and bypassed him as the prime minister, and he's shown that he sent him a report. So I certainly object, and it is a time and -- I mean, enormously time-wasting exercise because this is not a proper way to put the point across that you want to put across.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Ms. Korner has now mentioned reasons for the opposite. The only way to respond to the assertions by the prime minister that the minister of internal affairs didn't really work properly is to present to him the results of his work and argued by documents, not just by plain statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anyway, it's pastime for the break. We will resume in 20 minutes. Mr. Cvijetic, when you return you will remember the cautions that the Chamber has given you and the helpful advice that the Prosecutor has offered.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've been asked because of witness production schedules to establish how much longer this witness is likely to be. I understand about an hour to an hour and a half. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think I also need some time tomorrow, up to the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Which is a useful segue for saying, as the witness is on his way back in, that we don't propose to formally rule on Ms. Korner's objection beyond the observations that we would have already made, but Mr. Cvijetic would bear in mind the time limitation that he has, and also that at the end of the -- this witness's testimony the Chamber has to decide on the putting into effect the ruling that we would have given two weeks ago now as to what documents become exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. And I gather Mr. Pantelic is only going to be about five minutes with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, up to now. If something will arise, then I must react. And, Your Honours, I don't know if you are informed that I would like to address the Chamber at the end of this session for five minutes. I informed the registry, but if it's convenient, just for your knowledge. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, in compliance with, so to speak, informal decision of the Chamber in connection with the orders to the Ministry from the operative programme of the government, I will only say that the minister of the interior in this period issued rules on the disciplinary responsibility of employees of the organs of the interior in conditions of war and imminent threat of war, instructions on the rules of conduct and mutual relationships in the MUP, instructions on urgent ongoing statistical reporting of the Ministry of the Interior, binding instructions on actions to be taken by the Ministry of the Interior when carrying out search activities, instructions on reporting on the work of the ministry, and be prepared for adoption the most comprehensive document, the book of rules on the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior. To be quite honest, I thought of bringing it here to show you what a voluminous document it is. It has over 500 pages. Are you aware of all this, and are you aware of this activity of the Ministry of the Interior? Are you aware of any of this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, every ministry produced its own documentation, rules, and so on. It was their duty to do so. It was their obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And it also follows from the operational programme of the government.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the ministries.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, now I'm asking you in specific terms since I can't show these documents. Do you believe me that the minister adopted or issued all these documents?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to go into that. Why wouldn't I believe you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Cvijetic. The -- the -- your last question which the witness answered before I could raise a query, are you -- since you can't be giving evidence, are you inviting the witness to find -- to accept as a fact this list that you have put to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't see any third way. One way would be to show him each of these documents. You suggested that this would not be a good idea. Now I've read out to him a list of the documents which I assert were issued by the minister and which have been admitted into evidence. So I'm asking the witness whether he knows of the existence of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So they have been in evidence, is that the position? These are documents in evidence already. I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Your Honours -- Your Honours, all of them except the last one were introduced by way of the last witness and admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. Please proceed, but still there is -- I'm not sure that the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's no evidence before the Court other than any -- an assertion by Mr. Cvijetic as to who prepared the documents which are in evidence. They're in evidence. Mr. Cvijetic has asserted it. He's giving evidence. It's improper. And this witness can't -- why this witness should believe or disbelieve Mr. Cvijetic is a complete mystery to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, it's that last point that I wanted clarification on, whether the -- wouldn't it have been necessary for you to get an answer from this witness as to whether he accepted that list of documents or list of events as a fact before he could comment on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I've already asked him about this in a similar way.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric -- Mr. Djeric, you've heard the list of documents which I assert were issued by the minister. Do you accept this as a correct fact?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't want to go into that, because these documents on the internal organisation and so on were never something we disputed about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: So you think it is not in dispute that the minister issued these documents?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is the work of the services of the ministry, they had to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But apart from his obligation to issue documents, the minister also issued orders. Do you know about this method of work of the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that in that minister orders are issued. That's the nature of the ministry, that ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Some tasks from the operative programme of the government were implemented by the minister through his issuing of certain orders. I would like to show some of these orders now by which the minister implemented the tasks assigned to him. And later on, you can say whether these tasks follow from the operative plan and programme of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have 65 ter 356, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, in your binder it's document 27. I do apologise for not mentioning it before. Now, please read. Mr. Djeric, you will agree that before the adoption of the government programme the minister started implementing the tasks following from the law rather than the government programme? Do you agree with what I said, and can one see this from this order?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what orders the minister issued, so I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But now that you do see the order, can you agree with my conclusion that even before the government programme the minister started working on these tasks? Is this evident from this order? Yes or no, sir? Let's not waste time.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But you're asking me something -- you're asking me to say yes or no, but from my point of view the whole problem was in practice, in -- I see the order, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 65 ter 91, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, it's document 28 in your binder. Can you find your way in it? Within the scope of your assertion that in the beginning it was difficult even for the government to start functioning in lieu of all the problem we've mentioned, Mr. Djeric, the ministry also had its problems, even quite elementary ones. Do you see from this order that the minister dealt with securing elementary conditions for his work, and does this fit into what you said about the initial problems where you said that the state is being constructed on a meadow?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it might fit into that, but I have to say that it is the minister's job to take care of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at document 65 ter 358 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Professor. In your set of documents, that is number 29. I apologise. Yes, yes. That's it, 29. It's a little bit bad, the example, the copy, but anyway. Mr. Djeric, when a minister assumes his duties, he has to know what it says here. Amongst other things, he has to ask to be informed about the resources and the weaponry at the disposal of the public security stations that they are to work with. You would agree with me that perhaps that was one of the first tasks that he has to carry out so that he would know exactly what the means are at his disposal. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, let us go on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 360.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And according to me, perhaps this is something that a minister should have done first to see what sort of a police force was at his disposal. Can you please look at item one in paragraph one where he's trying to get the basic information, how many police stations there were. So all of that we can bring into context. You will agree with me with the inaccessibility of all of those territories?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Since the question was not in the transcript, I have to repeat it. Does that fit into the inaccessibility of specific territories so that the minister himself also has the same sort of problems that you referred to yourself?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That problem did exist. The problem did exist. As for this letter, I cannot say --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- whether that was caused by that or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because you can see from this letter that the minister is asking in order to be able to follow all the resources, he's seeking specific information.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. We're not going to spend any more time on that document. We're going to look at an order sent directly to the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we look at document 1D00-0507.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You've already opened document 31, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still don't have it in the BH version. All right. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you please read the document slowly. And can you please see who signed the document.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can see that Karadzic signed, the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I cannot see anything about two platoons of the police forces for special operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you look at the last sentence in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Inform the Presidency and the Supreme Command about the task that is implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And it says: "And resubordinate to the military command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You were talking about resubordination. Is this one of those forms of resubordination? When the supreme commander decides on the decision, that is why it says there are two platoons of the police and even it says to whom they should be resubordinated to; is that the answer you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if that is the way to do it like this two platoons and so on and so forth if this is done that way, but you know that police was resubordinated to the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Now let us look at the next document and the reaction of the minister to this order?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at document 1D00-0515 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You've already opened the document so can you please read it before we see it on the screen. It's 0515. All right. Can you please look at Mr. Stanisic's response a little bit. Mr. Stanisic says: "This ministry has acted pursuant to your command," it says, so he says that to the supreme commander, but from the text that continues, you can see and you can confirm that he is unwillingly acting pursuant to this order. Do you remember the efforts by the minister to withdraw from combat lines the policemen so that they could do their job? And he's even telling in some way, if I may put it that way, to the president.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were such efforts to ask for police for combat activities, but there was not enough of them over there. So no regular police work was being done.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are overlapping.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I think that the response to my previous question was not entered into the transcript, so I have to put the question again. Is that a problem that existed really in relation to the engagement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was that problem. It did exist, because the military sought through the president to have a part of the police participate in some operations, and this was not always met with approval for the simple reason that the ministry complained that they were also having difficulty with the shortage of men, and this is all I can say about it, nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Well, I hope everything's in the transcript now. Okay. I would like to move to the next document. This is 65 ter 180. You have that in your set of documents under 33? If something has not changed, that is that document. All right. Let's look at the first page. This is a document by the minister of internal affairs requesting all the centres look at this a little bit. "Send him all the information regarding, A, the activities of the paramilitary formations." Under B: "Information and data regarding police participation in combat actions when this was not necessary." You can see that. And then the number of policemen who took part, and so on. In the preamble or the introductory paragraph of this document, which you can look at, the minister states reasons for that which are the attempts to make certain distinctions and limitations with the military command and the military about the use of manpower. You say that this was a long-standing problem and that the minister persistently tried to resolve it.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was the problem about the jurisdiction between the police and the army, and it was constantly ongoing, and there were conflicts about that regarding actions in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right, one of the ways to resolve that would be this order to do this in a meeting and to define the jurisdictions more precisely?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were constant attempts to try to resolve this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at document -- I think it is Exhibit 1D58 of the court, meaning that it has already been admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And this is 34. That's where it is in the binder of documents in front of you. 1D58. Mr. Djeric, do you know about the activity of the ministry aimed at reducing the number of the reserve police and the elimination from their ranks of perpetrators of criminal acts or those who tended to do that? Do you have any information about that? Was this something that was discussed at government meetings?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were no particular information about that other than the order to the MUP to prosecute all perpetrators of crimes. As for what the minister did subsequent to that, I don't know. All I know is what the government sought to have done. So this would be some proof of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Just have some patience. So this order would then reflect the tendencies -- the intention of the government. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at 1D55.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And that's 35 in your binder. Isn't that right? Have you found it? Very well. The minister is dealing with the matter here of pronouncing a measure of detention and the manner that this will be done, and I'm going to remind you here about your testimony where you were making a difference between detention facilities. There is a legally regulated term of custody up to three days. Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there is also a kind of court custody?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You don't know that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's not up to me. I didn't deal with that. This is in the domain of the minister of justice and the minister of internal affairs the kind of detention and custody facilities that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. As part of their jurisdiction --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I would remind counsel and the witness to leave a suitable interval for the interpreters, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. You will agree, Mr. Djeric, that the minister was doing his job? He was carrying out duties that were part of his -- within his purview?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 65 ter 261. Can we please show that document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, that document is marked 36 in your binder. Do you have that document? Perhaps it's been mislaid somewhere. That's it. Yes, yes. Just go ahead and open it. That's it. In the agenda and in the decisions of the government, I found that the government dealt with the problem of the reduction of the number of the police reserve force. Did you deal with that matter? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, as you can see, this order is going in that direction in light of that line that the minister wished to protect his work. He decided to place at the disposal of the military reserve policemen and to relieve active policemen from front duty so that they could carry on with their regular duties. Is that along the line of what you were talking about, the constant struggle in that sense? Was there a constant conflict about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the way things were going on this was not something that the government was dealing with, this was between the police and the military. And I know from talks that there was often conflict between the ministry of the police and the army, and from some government meetings there were conclusions that the two ministers should sit down and the police and the military should sit down and agree about the lines of jurisdiction among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Djeric, as part of the attempt to suppress all types of crime, it was the job of the ministry to investigate all the cases that it was able to investigate and to resolve them, especially those where the victims were non-Serbs. I think that you also talked about that, that there were such cases where these proceedings had to be completed.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a request of the government for such perpetrators to be prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to take you through one case and then later through a couple of others.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please open document -- this is your document 37. So it's 1D00-617. 0617. Just a moment until we find the electronic version. There it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you looked at this authorisation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Dragan Andan, an inspector of the police administration was tasked with touring the public security stations, police stations to inspect their work, offer professional advice, and so on. I'll go through the result of one such visit as we don't have time to deal with all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at the next document, 65 ter 194.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's 38 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And please go on to the next page both in B/C/S and English. This is just the cover letter. So let's go and look at the information in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: -- have you had a chance to leaf through this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: What did Mr. Dragan Andan find in Bijeljina, for example? It's in the middle of the first paragraph, so go back to the first page where it says "Information." It says, the paramilitary units, and so on and so forth. And on that same page in passage three, he says: "The population, both Muslims and Serbs, are being terrorised. There are cases of rape, looting. Over ten persons of different nationalities have been killed." You see that? "Without any evident motive. All these cases remain unresolved," and so on and so forth. On the next page -- we can move on to page 2. On the next page. On page 2 Mr. Andan is speaking about what specifically he found in the police station, what steps he took for the situation to improve. Look at the footnote on page 3. "Because of abuse of illegal work and so on, 17 employees have been removed." Is that right? Could you please look at the date when this was written. The Ministry of the Interior, you will agree, is putting in order the situation on the ground by sending inspectors to improve it. Are you aware of this form of work of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was how the government worked, to look for information. As regards the quality of that information, it varied, but first of all, proposals of measures were sought. You see that there are no such proposals in this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Yes, on page 3 --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what was done, but I am referring to proposals for measures to be taken by the government, because the inspector was there, but there are no measures proposed for the government to take --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, be patient and we'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a typical inspector's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My question was -- well, it's the 29th of July, if I'm not wrong. May I now show you a document? It's 39 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 65 ter 1285.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Dragan Andan, you'll see in the signature below, as the chief is processing the case of the first international murder in Bijeljina -- or rather, inter-ethnic murder in Bijeljina. The perpetrators were discovered. They were brought in and handed over to the appropriate prosecutor's office, along with a criminal report. Would you agree that this form of work of the ministry did yield results? You were talking about practical results. Well, here they are. And all the other ten murders were also dealt with you will see. So this is a response to what you said before.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was what the government insisted on, on this way of working to prosecute these people and prove that they've been prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Djeric, I've shown you one example. I think we'll be dealing with larger cases than this, but now I'd like to move on to another topic, and that's the problem of detention, collection centres, camps, and prisons. You say that this was an ongoing problem that both you and the government and the Presidency dealt with on an ongoing basis.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the government. The government ordered the Ministry of Justice and the Ministry of the Interior to do things, but we couldn't issue orders to the army. It was others who were in charge of the army, not us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Please pause before you answer my question for the sake of the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have document which has been admitted into evidence, 1D56.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Where is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's your document 40A, right after 40. It's handwritten. That's it. I think that's it. Yes. Have you found it, 1D56? It's an exhibit. Have you read the order?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's this? I can't find what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It's 40A. It's next one. That's it.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't see that it says "Order" here to the chief personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: It says down below, "I order." That's why I called it an order. It's an order by which the minister is establishing how prisoners of war and the civilian population should be treated, as well as refugees. And this should be done exclusively in compliance with the law, the competencies of the MUP, and the provisions of international law and international conventions. That's all in paragraph one. And paragraph two deals with the gathering of information on so-called ad hoc prisons and camps, and then all those who violate these rules and international conventions, they're to be prosecuted. So did this order follow from the decisions of the government?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can conclude that it referred -- or, rather, relied upon the government's decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The next document is an exhibit. In your binder it's 41, and it's Exhibit 1D57. Have you managed to read the document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of Health were -- Labour and Social Welfare is applying to the security services, and it says here: "The following information must be delivered regardless of jurisdiction." The minister acted on this request from the health ministry regardless of jurisdiction and ordered that this information be gathered, the information mentioned here. I have to ask you again. Does this manner of working fit into the government's normal ways of proceeding, that the ministries should co-operate and exchange information? Briefly. There's not much time. It's a question that has to do with the government.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the government, Dragan Kalinic, who was the Minister of Health, he was the president of the republic, and I assume that that's where his letter came from sent to the Ministry of the Interior, because at that time there was a lot of media attention, and the president designated Mr. Kalinic to coordinate with the UNHCR, and that's how this came about.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, I'll go back to the government's operative plan. Could you please look at 41A. Look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's 1D63. I think it's already an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Can you see what this is about? Within the scope of the tasks taken by the ministry -- undertaken by the ministry and documenting war crimes, the minister, along with what you see here on page 1, forwarded to all the centres --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's turn to page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: -- questionnaire.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page. It's a document with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Do you see this questionnaire?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'll draw your attention to some questions in this questionnaire. So it deals with data on victims, and in item 5 you can see that the document is not selective as regards to the ethnicity of the victim. It refers to all victims. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, all ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said that that was how the government dealt with the problem; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, since we're on the topic of these centres for the custody of persons, I would now like to open minutes from a government session which you have under 43 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this is Exhibit -- 65 ter 1188.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you found it, 43? Is that it? Let's see if we have the real -- the proper document here. This is a session of the 10th of June, 1992. In the Serbian version, on page 2, if you would be kind enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on page 3 of the English version, at the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And do you see "Current issues." Open questions. There is a conclusion that the Ministry of Justice should prepare a report on the detained persons where the treatment of the civilian population, prisoners of war, accommodation, food, and so on, would be treated as a separate topic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And that information would be reviewed by you, the government, and then by the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And it's clear in terms of the jurisdiction as well, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. This problem, isn't it right, was tackled by the government, also by forming a commission to tour the collection centres and other facilities in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the practice, the practice for the ministries that were responsible to take care of the collection centres and so on and so forth, and as needed, the government would form a commission. I remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Oh, that is document -- I apologise. Is that 45 in your binder?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And it's 65 ter 210. I apologise to the registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: With this decision a commission was formed to tour the collection centres, and its task was to submit a report to the government as can be seen in item 3. And that is 45 in your binder. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This decision?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you found it? All right. Do you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember it. I think that the commission, and there were even commissions -- actually, I remember the commission. Not everything, but I know that Slobodan Aviljas was in that commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did it do its job, and did they do a report for you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commission made a report which was --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just be patient. Just be patient, because it's under a different number.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 215. Can we have that opened, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here's the report, and I think that it has not been completed. I think there is a page missing, the signature page.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Possibly. 215. Let me have a look. Let's go to the bottom of the screen to see if that is that. Let's see the signature. Let's see what the last page is. I am interested in paragraph 4. All right. Evidently -- I mean, it's obvious there are no signatures, but that is that report; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the practice was that the commission member submitting the report would put their signatures.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. Well, this page that we have on the screen here, and the paragraph marked 4 where it says that the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of the Interior shall take measures to ensure that all the above facilities are handed over to the army and the Serbian Republic. Do you remember that conclusion? If you don't, you can just say that you don't.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, this was probably the conclusion that was reached, but I'm a little bit confused because there is no page, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. We will try to find this page. Obviously it wasn't published, but I think it exists. We will find it. Mr. Djeric --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: -- I'm now going to just go through some of those facilities if we have time so that tomorrow we don't have to deal with this issue so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now open document --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And in your binder that is document 47, Mr. Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we can have 65 ter opened, 1463.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you see what this is about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You know what the camp in Vlasenica was called. Can you please tell us what the camp in Vlasenica was called? If you don't know --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: We can see here that it is an exclusively military camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was formed by the military and the military was in charge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, that is just enough for us to be able to conclude that. I like to move to the next document that is document 48 in your set of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that is 65 ter 381 for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Have you opened it?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: At the bottom you can see 48.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Is it -- Mr. Djeric, the previous one it says that it's not in the transcript, who was in charge of that camp the one in Vlasenica? Just repeat it, I'm not going to suggest anything to you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see from here from the order that it was the army, that the army, the military formed that camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. Now, we will go back to, which is yours, 48. So we have a centre just like that here in Hadzici; is that correct? Do you see that is document 48, and the Ministry of Justice is dealing with it, all right? Well, yes, I'm being told now that I'm going too fast again. Thus this centre in Hadzici is under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Justice, your minister, and he is asking for these persons to be transferred to the penitentiary in Butmir. Do you know anything about that transfer?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO DJERIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know anything, so I don't know what the Ministry of Justice was doing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, you know, I'm really sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm going to go on repeating this. This is not a proper exercise. Counsel giving evidence, reading documents, and the witness saying don't know anything about it for the majority. It's just not the way of dealing with evidence. And, Your Honour, if I hear there's an hour and a half more of this tomorrow, Your Honour, I repeat my objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can provide reasons. I am trying with the witness to determine what the responsibility was for these facilities through documents. I'm not testifying. I'm simply showing the document and then putting a question on the basis of the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just look at the question. "Do you know anything about that transfer?" "No, I don't know anything, so I don't know what the Ministry of Justice was doing." And that's been virtually the same answer for every single document with a couple of exceptions. If there was some proper informed choice being made and only documents about which the witness can speak to were being put, then I wouldn't be raising this objection, but this really is an appalling waste of everybody's time. Including, I may say, Mr. Djeric's.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Cvijetic, while you consider again these issues you would recall with your colleague Mr. Pantelic asked for five minutes before we rise today, so perhaps this would be a convenient point at which we should take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric, your testimony continues, and again I caution you, as I have at each adjournment, not to discuss the case with counsel from either side or -- not to speak with counsel or discuss the case with anyone outside the court. So you're excused to return to this Chamber at 2.15 tomorrow afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know you'd prefer this to be done by agreement, but it's not going to be done by agreement, and unless you do make a ruling, it's quite plain that Mr. Cvijetic is going to carry on doing just what he's been doing, so I just leave that with you overnight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I will allow myself overnight to decide how to deal with this. Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Your Honour, for understanding. Just one technical issue I would like to raise. We are, as far as I'm informed we are sitting on Friday in the afternoon from 2.15 until 7.00. At the same time I checked the availability of the courtrooms and apparently there is a place at the same courtroom, Courtroom I in the morning. So I kindly ask you to consider -- I was speaking with my learned friends from the Prosecution and other members if we could maybe move our session from afternoon Friday to morning Friday just without any -- any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do you have a particular problem with Friday afternoon, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: No, no, we don't have, but simply in terms of our organisation of our teams and some -- some plans that we have to -- to work. I mean, it's completely up to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I fully understand, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. This is a kind of telepathy. So I kindly ask our friends from the registry and the other services to see if we can do something on that matter. And I would like also to address Trial Chamber with regard to the other issue, but I would prefer to go in private session, please, if it's possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
